item.title: BIND 9 Authoritative and Recursive DNS
item.description:
BIND 9 runs the named name server. Its configuration determines whether it answers authoritatively, offers recursion, transfers zones, or accepts dynamic updates. Treat those roles separately because an Internet-facing authoritative server should not become an open recursive resolver.

Server Configuration #

named.conf defines global options, access-control lists, zones, and logging. A minimal authoritative configuration restricts recursion and zone transfer:

named 
acl trusted-recursors { 192.0.2.0/24; 2001:db8:1::/48; };

options {
 directory "/var/named";
 listen-on { any; };
 listen-on-v6 { any; };
 recursion no;
 allow-transfer { none; };
 minimal-responses yes;
};

zone "example.net" {
 type primary;
 file "zones/example.net";
 allow-transfer { 192.0.2.53; };
};

A recursive resolver needs recursion yes and an allow-recursion or allow-query-cache ACL limited to its clients. Never expose recursion to untrusted networks unless the deployment explicitly provides a public resolver with abuse controls.

item.title: Content Delivery Networks
item.description:
A content delivery network (CDN) serves content from edge locations close to users. It can cache static assets and, depending on the provider, proxy dynamic traffic, terminate TLS, filter attacks, and optimize connections. The origin remains the authoritative application; the CDN is an intermediary with an explicit caching and routing policy.

Connect a Domain to a CDN #

An operator configures an origin, such as https://origin.example.net, and creates a CDN distribution for www.example.com. The provider supplies a hostname such as example.cdnprovider.net; the operator then creates a DNS record that directs www.example.com to it, usually a CNAME:

item.title: DNS Wire Format
item.description:
DNS queries and responses begin with a 12-byte header followed by Question, Answer, Authority, and Additional sections. All multi-octet integer fields use network byte order. RFC 1035 defines the base format; EDNS, DNSSEC, and later extensions add records and header semantics without changing the base header.

Header #

Field Bits Purpose
ID 16 Client-selected identifier echoed in the response
QR 1 Query (0) or response (1)
Opcode 4 Operation; QUERY is zero
AA 1 Authoritative answer indicator in responses
TC 1 Message was truncated
RD 1 Client requests recursion
RA 1 Server offers recursion
Z 3 Reserved base bits; extensions use AD and CD
RCODE 4 Base response code
QDCOUNT 16 Question count
ANCOUNT 16 Answer record count
NSCOUNT 16 Authority record count
ARCOUNT 16 Additional record count

RD asks the receiving server to perform recursion; RA advertises that the server can do so. AA says the responding server is authoritative for the answer, not that every record in the message is authoritative. TC tells a client that it must retry over TCP or another supported transport when the truncated response is insufficient.

item.title: DNS Resolution Model
item.description:
DNS names form a rooted tree. A domain is the subtree rooted at a name. A zone is an administrative portion of that tree served as authoritative data. Domain and zone are therefore not synonyms: a zone can delegate a child subtree and no longer contain its authoritative records.

Delegation and Authority #

The parent zone delegates child.example. by publishing NS records at that name. The child zone publishes its own apex SOA and NS records. A resolver asking the parent for data below that cut receives a referral with the child’s NS RRset in the Authority section.

item.title: DNS and Anycast
item.description:
DNS is a distributed database whose keys are structured names. Its hierarchy lets administrators divide both data storage and responsibility: no organization must maintain every mapping, and an organization can delegate a subordinate namespace to another administrator. The same hierarchy also supplies a path by which a resolver can find the server that is authoritative for an unknown name.

The Hierarchical Namespace and Domains #

The DNS namespace is a rooted tree. Every node has a label of zero to 63 octets; siblings cannot have equal labels, although unrelated nodes can. The root has the zero-length, or null, label.
